docs.title: Kernel Target Alignment
docs.text:
Question: How well does a kernel K match the task (target labels)?

Kernel Alignment measures the similarity between kernel matrix K and the ideal kernel Y·Yᵀ:

Alignment(K, y) = ⟨K, y·yᵀ⟩_F / (||K||_F · ||y·yᵀ||_F)

where ⟨·,·⟩_F is Frobenius inner product: ⟨A,B⟩_F = Σᵢⱼ Aᵢⱼ Bᵢⱼ
      ||A||_F is Frobenius norm: ||A||_F = √(Σᵢⱼ Aᵢⱼ²)

Range: [-1, +1]
  +1 = perfect alignment (kernel perfectly matches labels)
   0 = no correlation
  -1 = perfectly anti-aligned

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification, make_moons, make_circles
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# ============================================================
# KERNEL ALIGNMENT
# ============================================================

def kernel_target_alignment(K, y):
    """
    Compute alignment between kernel matrix K and target y.

    Returns:
        alignment (float): Value in [-1, +1]
    """
    n = len(y)

    # Center y to {-1, +1}
    y_pm = np.where(y == 0, -1, 1).reshape(-1, 1)

    # Ideal kernel: Y·Yᵀ
    Y = y_pm @ y_pm.T

    # Frobenius inner product
    numerator   = np.sum(K * Y)
    denominator = np.sqrt(np.sum(K**2)) * np.sqrt(np.sum(Y**2))

    alignment = numerator / (denominator + 1e-10)

    return alignment


def compute_all_alignments(X, y, kernels_dict):
    """Compute alignment for multiple kernels."""
    results = {}

    for name, k_func in kernels_dict.items():
        n = len(X)
        K = np.array([[k_func(X[i], X[j]) for j in range(n)]
                      for i in range(n)])
        align = kernel_target_alignment(K, y)
        results[name] = align

    return results


print("="*60)
print("KERNEL-TARGET ALIGNMENT")
print("="*60)

# Test on different datasets
datasets = [
    ("Linear Sep", *make_classification(n_samples=100, n_features=2,
                                        n_redundant=0, n_informative=2,
                                        class_sep=2.5, random_state=42)),
    ("Moons", *make_moons(n_samples=100, noise=0.2, random_state=42)),
    ("Circles", *make_circles(n_samples=100, noise=0.1,
                              factor=0.4, random_state=42)),
]

kernels_test = {
    'Linear':    lambda x, xp: np.dot(x, xp),
    'Poly d=2':  lambda x, xp: (np.dot(x, xp) + 1)**2,
    'Poly d=3':  lambda x, xp: (np.dot(x, xp) + 1)**3,
    'RBF γ=0.5': lambda x, xp: np.exp(-0.5 * np.sum((x-xp)**2)),
    'RBF γ=1.0': lambda x, xp: np.exp(-1.0 * np.sum((x-xp)**2)),
    'RBF γ=2.0': lambda x, xp: np.exp(-2.0 * np.sum((x-xp)**2)),
}

all_results = {}

for ds_name, X_ds, y_ds in datasets:
    X_s = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_ds)
    alignments = compute_all_alignments(X_s, y_ds, kernels_test)
    all_results[ds_name] = alignments

    print(f"\n--- {ds_name} ---")
    for k_name in sorted(alignments, key=alignments.get, reverse=True):
        align = alignments[k_name]
        print(f"  {k_name:<15}: {align:>7.4f}")


# ============================================================
# VISUALIZE ALIGNMENT
# ============================================================

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))

for ax, ds_name in zip(axes, all_results.keys()):
    alignments = all_results[ds_name]

    names  = list(alignments.keys())
    values = [alignments[n] for n in names]
    colors = ['green' if v > 0.7 else 'orange' if v > 0.4 else 'red'
              for v in values]

    bars = ax.barh(range(len(names)), values, color=colors, alpha=0.7,
                   edgecolor='k')
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(names)))
    ax.set_yticklabels(names, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel('Alignment')
    ax.set_title(f'{ds_name}\n(Higher = better match to labels)')
    ax.axvline(x=0, color='black', linewidth=1)
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3, axis='x')
    ax.set_xlim(-0.2, 1.0)

plt.suptitle('Kernel-Target Alignment Comparison\n'
             'Green (>0.7) = Excellent, Orange (>0.4) = Good, Red = Poor',
             fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('kernel_alignment.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("\nSaved: kernel_alignment.png")


print("\n" + "="*60)
print("INTERPRETATION")
print("="*60)
print("""
Kernel-target alignment helps you choose the right kernel BEFORE training:

1. Compute alignment for candidate kernels
2. Choose kernel with highest alignment
3. This kernel is most "compatible" with the classification task

Note: High alignment ≠ guaranteed good performance
      But it's a useful heuristic for kernel selection
""")

docs.title: RBF Kernel: The Infinite-Dimensional Case
docs.text:
RBF Kernel: K(x, x') = exp(-γ||x - x'||²)

Taylor expansion of exp():
  exp(z) = 1 + z + z²/2! + z³/3! + ...

This gives an INFINITE series of polynomial terms!
→ Feature map φ(x) has infinitely many dimensions

Yet K(x, x') can be computed in O(d) time where d = input dimension!

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ============================================================
# RBF: INFINITE FEATURE SPACE
# ============================================================

print("="*60)
print("RBF KERNEL: INFINITE-DIMENSIONAL FEATURE SPACE")
print("="*60)

print("""
RBF kernel: K(x, x') = exp(-γ||x - x'||²)

Expanding:
  exp(-γ||x - x'||²)
  = exp(-γ||x||²) · exp(2γ xᵀx') · exp(-γ||x'||²)

The middle term exp(2γ xᵀx') has Taylor expansion:
  exp(2γ xᵀx') = Σₙ₌₀^∞ (2γ)ⁿ/(n!) · (xᵀx')ⁿ

This is a weighted sum of ALL polynomial degrees!
→ Infinite-dimensional feature space

Each degree n contributes with weight (2γ)ⁿ/n!
""")

# Show weight decay
gammas = [0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0]
degrees = np.arange(0, 20)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))

for gamma in gammas:
    weights = [(2*gamma)**n / np.math.factorial(n)
               for n in degrees]
    plt.plot(degrees, weights, 'o-', linewidth=2,
             label=f'γ = {gamma}')

plt.xlabel('Polynomial Degree n')
plt.ylabel('Weight = (2γ)ⁿ / n!')
plt.title('RBF Kernel: Contribution by Polynomial Degree\n'
          'All degrees contribute → infinite-dimensional')
plt.legend()
plt.yscale('log')
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('rbf_infinite_weights.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("Saved: rbf_infinite_weights.png")

print("\nKey insight:")
print("  Smaller γ → more weight on higher degrees → more complex")
print("  Larger γ → weight concentrated on lower degrees → simpler")


# ============================================================
# FINITE APPROXIMATION
# ============================================================

print("\n\n" + "="*60)
print("FINITE-RANK APPROXIMATION OF RBF")
print("="*60)

def rbf_truncated(x, xp, gamma=1.0, max_degree=5):
    """
    Approximate RBF using first max_degree terms of Taylor series.
    """
    dot = np.dot(x, xp)

    # exp(-γ||x||²) * exp(-γ||x'||²) * Σ (2γ)ⁿ/n! (xᵀx')ⁿ
    norm_x  = np.exp(-gamma * np.dot(x, x))
    norm_xp = np.exp(-gamma * np.dot(xp, xp))

    poly_sum = sum((2*gamma)**n / np.math.factorial(n) * dot**n
                   for n in range(max_degree + 1))

    return norm_x * norm_xp * poly_sum


# Compare exact vs truncated
np.random.seed(42)
X_approx = np.random.randn(10, 2)

print(f"\n{'Degree limit':<15} {'Max |error|':<15} {'Mean |error|'}")
print("-" * 45)

for max_deg in [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20]:
    errors = []
    for i in range(len(X_approx)):
        for j in range(len(X_approx)):
            k_exact = k_rbf(X_approx[i], X_approx[j])
            k_trunc = rbf_truncated(X_approx[i], X_approx[j],
                                   gamma=0.5, max_degree=max_deg)
            errors.append(abs(k_exact - k_trunc))

    print(f"{max_deg:<15} {max(errors):<15.2e} {np.mean(errors):.2e}")

print("\nConclusion: Even with 10-20 terms, approximation is excellent!")
print("But RBF kernel computes exact value in O(d) time")

docs.title: Why Normalize?
docs.text:
Normalizing a kernel ensures K(x,x) = 1 for all x:

K_normalized(x, x') = K(x, x') / √(K(x,x) · K(x',x'))

Benefits:
  - Scale-invariant: K̃(cx, cx') = K̃(x, x') for any c > 0
  - Bounded: -1 ≤ K̃(x, x') ≤ 1
  - Interpretable as cosine similarity in feature space

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ============================================================
# KERNEL NORMALIZATION
# ============================================================

def normalize_kernel(K_func):
    """
    Return normalized version of a kernel function.
    K̃(x,x') = K(x,x') / √(K(x,x)·K(x',x'))
    """
    def K_normalized(x, xp):
        k_xx  = K_func(x, x)
        k_xpxp = K_func(xp, xp)
        k_xxp  = K_func(x, xp)
        return k_xxp / (np.sqrt(k_xx * k_xpxp) + 1e-10)

    return K_normalized


print("="*60)
print("KERNEL NORMALIZATION")
print("="*60)

# Original kernels
k_poly_unnorm = lambda x, xp: (np.dot(x, xp) + 1)**2
k_rbf_unnorm  = lambda x, xp: np.exp(-0.5 * np.sum((x - xp)**2))

# Normalized versions
k_poly_norm = normalize_kernel(k_poly_unnorm)
k_rbf_norm  = normalize_kernel(k_rbf_unnorm)

# Test points
np.random.seed(42)
x_test  = np.array([1.0, 2.0])
xp_test = np.array([3.0, -1.0])

print("\nPolynomial Kernel (degree 2):")
print(f"  Original K(x,x'):    {k_poly_unnorm(x_test, xp_test):.4f}")
print(f"  Normalized K̃(x,x'): {k_poly_norm(x_test, xp_test):.4f}")
print(f"  K̃(x,x):             {k_poly_norm(x_test, x_test):.4f}  (= 1 always)")
print(f"  K̃(x',x'):           {k_poly_norm(xp_test, xp_test):.4f}  (= 1 always)")

print("\nRBF Kernel:")
print(f"  Original K(x,x'):    {k_rbf_unnorm(x_test, xp_test):.4f}")
print(f"  Normalized K̃(x,x'): {k_rbf_norm(x_test, xp_test):.4f}")
print(f"  K̃(x,x):             {k_rbf_norm(x_test, x_test):.4f}  (= 1 always)")


# ============================================================
# VISUALIZATION: Before vs After Normalization
# ============================================================

X_norm = np.random.randn(20, 2) * np.array([1, 5])  # Different scales

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(15, 10))

for col, (name, k_orig, k_norm) in enumerate([
    ("Polynomial", k_poly_unnorm, k_poly_norm),
    ("RBF", k_rbf_unnorm, k_rbf_norm),
]):
    # Original kernel matrix
    K_orig = np.array([[k_orig(X_norm[i], X_norm[j])
                        for j in range(len(X_norm))]
                       for i in range(len(X_norm))])

    # Normalized kernel matrix
    K_norm_mat = np.array([[k_norm(X_norm[i], X_norm[j])
                            for j in range(len(X_norm))]
                           for i in range(len(X_norm))])

    # Plot original
    ax = axes[0, col]
    im = ax.imshow(K_orig, cmap='viridis', aspect='auto')
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046)
    ax.set_title(f'{name}\nOriginal')

    diag_orig = np.diag(K_orig)
    ax.text(0.5, -0.15, f'Diagonal range: [{diag_orig.min():.2f}, {diag_orig.max():.2f}]',
            transform=ax.transAxes, ha='center', fontsize=9)

    # Plot normalized
    ax = axes[1, col]
    im = ax.imshow(K_norm_mat, cmap='viridis', aspect='auto', vmin=-1, vmax=1)
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046)
    ax.set_title(f'{name}\nNormalized')

    diag_norm = np.diag(K_norm_mat)
    ax.text(0.5, -0.15, f'Diagonal: all = 1.00',
            transform=ax.transAxes, ha='center', fontsize=9,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor='lightgreen', alpha=0.5))

# Comparison panel
ax = axes[0, 2]
ax.text(0.5, 0.5,
        "NORMALIZATION EFFECT:\n\n"
        "Before:\n"
        "• K(x,x) varies\n"
        "• Scale-dependent\n"
        "• Unbounded range\n\n"
        "After:\n"
        "• K̃(x,x) = 1 always\n"
        "• Scale-invariant\n"
        "• Range: [-1, +1]\n"
        "• = cosine similarity",
        ha='center', va='center', fontsize=11,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor='wheat', alpha=0.8))
ax.axis('off')

ax = axes[1, 2]
ax.axis('off')

plt.suptitle('Kernel Normalization',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('kernel_normalization.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("\nSaved: kernel_normalization.png")

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
STATIONARY KERNEL:
  K(x, x') = f(x - x')  or  f(||x - x'||)

  Depends only on the difference or distance between points
  → Translation-invariant: K(x+c, x'+c) = K(x, x')

  Examples: RBF, Laplacian, Matérn

NON-STATIONARY KERNEL:
  K(x, x') = f(x, x')  (general function of both arguments)

  Can vary across input space

  Examples: Linear, Polynomial, Neural network kernels

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ============================================================
# STATIONARY VS NON-STATIONARY
# ============================================================

print("="*60)
print("STATIONARY VS NON-STATIONARY KERNELS")
print("="*60)

# Test translation invariance
x1  = np.array([0.0, 0.0])
x1p = np.array([1.0, 1.0])

shift = np.array([10.0, 5.0])
x2  = x1 + shift
x2p = x1p + shift

print("\nOriginal points:")
print(f"  x = {x1}, x' = {x1p}")
print(f"\nShifted points (+{shift}):")
print(f"  x = {x2}, x' = {x2p}")

kernels_test_stat = [
    ("RBF (stationary)", k_rbf, True),
    ("Laplacian (stationary)", k_laplacian, True),
    ("Linear (non-stationary)", k_linear, False),
    ("Polynomial (non-stationary)", k_poly, False),
]

print(f"\n{'Kernel':<30} {'K(x,x\')':<12} {'K(x+c,x\'+c)':<15} {'Invariant?'}")
print("-"*70)

for name, k_fn, expected_stat in kernels_test_stat:
    k_orig = k_fn(x1, x1p)
    k_shift = k_fn(x2, x2p)
    is_invariant = np.isclose(k_orig, k_shift)

    status = "✓" if is_invariant == expected_stat else "✗"
    print(f"{name:<30} {k_orig:<12.4f} {k_shift:<15.4f} {status}")


# ============================================================
# VISUALIZE: Kernel values across space
# ============================================================

# Fix one point at origin
x_fixed = np.array([0.0, 0.0])

# Scan over a grid
x_range = np.linspace(-3, 3, 50)
X_grid, Y_grid = np.meshgrid(x_range, x_range)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 12))

kernels_viz_stat = [
    ("RBF (Stationary)", k_rbf),
    ("Laplacian (Stationary)", k_laplacian),
    ("Linear (Non-stationary)", k_linear),
    ("Polynomial d=2 (Non-stationary)", k_poly),
]

for ax, (name, k_fn) in zip(axes.ravel(), kernels_viz_stat):
    K_vals = np.zeros_like(X_grid)
    for i in range(len(x_range)):
        for j in range(len(x_range)):
            x_test = np.array([X_grid[j, i], Y_grid[j, i]])
            K_vals[j, i] = k_fn(x_fixed, x_test)

    cf = ax.contourf(X_grid, Y_grid, K_vals, levels=20, cmap='viridis')
    plt.colorbar(cf, ax=ax)

    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    ax.axis('equal')

             'Stationary = circular/radial contours (translation-invariant)\n'
             'Non-stationary = arbitrary contours',
             fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A kernel K is universal if the RKHS it induces is dense in C(X), the space of continuous functions on a compact domain X.

Practical meaning: A universal kernel can approximate any continuous function arbitrarily well (given enough data).

Universal kernels include: - RBF (Gaussian) - Laplacian - Matérn (for ν > 0)

Not universal: - Linear - Polynomial (finite degree)

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.kernel_ridge import KernelRidge

# ============================================================
# UNIVERSAL KERNELS: APPROXIMATION POWER
# ============================================================

print("="*60)
print("UNIVERSAL KERNELS")
print("="*60)

print("""
Theorem (Micchelli, 1986; Steinwart, 2001):
  The RBF kernel is universal on ℝᵈ for any γ > 0.

  This means: Given enough data and proper regularization,
              RBF-based methods can approximate any continuous
              function arbitrarily well.

This is why RBF is the default choice for kernel methods!
""")

# Test approximation of a complex function
np.random.seed(42)
n_train = 50

def complex_function(x):
    """A complex target function to approximate."""
    return np.sin(4*x) + 0.3*np.sin(12*x) + 0.5*np.cos(6*x)

X_train = np.sort(np.random.uniform(0, 5, n_train)).reshape(-1, 1)
y_train = complex_function(X_train.ravel()) + np.random.randn(n_train) * 0.1

X_test = np.linspace(0, 5, 300).reshape(-1, 1)
y_true = complex_function(X_test.ravel())

# Try different kernels
kernels_univ = [
    ('Linear (not universal)', 'linear', {}),
    ('Polynomial d=3 (not universal)', 'poly', {'degree': 3, 'coef0': 1}),
    ('RBF γ=1 (universal)', 'rbf', {'gamma': 1.0}),
    ('RBF γ=5 (universal)', 'rbf', {'gamma': 5.0}),
    ('Laplacian (universal)', 'laplacian', {}),
]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(18, 10))
axes = axes.ravel()

for ax, (name, kernel, params) in zip(axes, kernels_univ):
    if kernel == 'laplacian':
        # sklearn doesn't have laplacian, use additive_chi2 as proxy
        # or implement custom
        kr = KernelRidge(kernel='rbf', alpha=0.01, gamma=1.0)
    else:
        kr = KernelRidge(kernel=kernel, alpha=0.01, **params)

    kr.fit(X_train, y_train)
    y_pred = kr.predict(X_test)

    mse = np.mean((y_pred - y_true)**2)

    ax.scatter(X_train, y_train, c='gray', s=20, alpha=0.7,
               label='Training data')
    ax.plot(X_test, y_true, 'g-', linewidth=2, label='True function')
    ax.plot(X_test, y_pred, 'r--', linewidth=2, label='Prediction')
    ax.set_xlabel('x')
    ax.set_ylabel('y')
    ax.set_title(f'{name}\nMSE = {mse:.4f}')
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Summary panel
ax = axes[-1]
ax.text(0.5, 0.5,
        "UNIVERSAL KERNELS:\n\n"
        "Can approximate\nANY continuous function\n\n"
        "→ RBF succeeds where\n"
        "   linear & polynomial fail\n\n"
        "→ This is theoretical guarantee\n"
        "   of approximation power\n\n"
        "→ Practical: use RBF as default!",
        ha='center', va='center', fontsize=12,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor='lightgreen', alpha=0.8))
ax.axis('off')

plt.suptitle('Universal Kernels: Function Approximation Power\n'
             'Universal kernels can approximate any continuous function',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('universal_kernels.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("\nSaved: universal_kernels.png")

docs.title: Key Concepts Recap
docs.text:
print("="*70)
print("KERNEL FUNCTIONS: KEY CONCEPTS")
print("="*70)

concepts = """
1. VALID KERNEL ⟺ POSITIVE SEMI-DEFINITE
   - Kernel matrix K has all eigenvalues ≥ 0
   - Equivalently: there exists feature map φ such that K(x,x') = ⟨φ(x),φ(x')⟩

2. ESSENTIAL PROPERTIES
   - Symmetry: K(x,x') = K(x',x)
   - PSD: vᵀKv ≥ 0 for all v
   - Cauchy-Schwarz: |K(x,x')|² ≤ K(x,x)·K(x',x')

3. COMPOSITION RULES
   - Sum: K₁ + K₂
   - Product: K₁ · K₂
   - Scaling: c·K (c > 0)
   - Polynomial: (K + c)ᵈ
   - Exponential: exp(K)
   → All preserve validity!

4. FEATURE MAPS
   - Explicit (polynomial): compute φ(x) directly
   - Implicit (RBF): φ(x) has infinite dimensions, never computed

5. NORMALIZATION
   - K̃(x,x') = K(x,x') / √(K(x,x)·K(x',x'))
   - Ensures K̃(x,x) = 1
   - Bounded: -1 ≤ K̃ ≤ 1

6. STATIONARY KERNELS
   - K(x,x') = f(x - x')
   - Translation-invariant
   - Examples: RBF, Laplacian, Matérn

7. UNIVERSAL KERNELS
   - Can approximate any continuous function
   - RBF, Laplacian are universal
   - Linear, polynomial are NOT universal

8. KERNEL ALIGNMENT
   - Measures how well K matches target labels
   - Range: [-1, +1]
   - Useful for kernel selection
"""

print(concepts)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A radial basis function is any function φ: ℝ → ℝ whose value depends only on the distance from a center point:

φ(x) = φ(||x - c||)

Where:
  x = input point
  c = center
  ||·|| = distance (typically Euclidean)

"Radial" = depends only on radius (distance)
"Basis" = can be used as basis functions for function approximation

docs.title: Common RBF Types
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ============================================================
# RADIAL BASIS FUNCTIONS: COMMON TYPES
# ============================================================

def rbf_gaussian(r, epsilon=1.0):
    """Gaussian RBF: φ(r) = exp(-ε²r²)"""
    return np.exp(-epsilon**2 * r**2)

def rbf_multiquadric(r, epsilon=1.0):
    """Multiquadric: φ(r) = √(1 + (εr)²)"""
    return np.sqrt(1 + (epsilon * r)**2)

def rbf_inverse_multiquadric(r, epsilon=1.0):
    """Inverse Multiquadric: φ(r) = 1/√(1 + (εr)²)"""
    return 1.0 / np.sqrt(1 + (epsilon * r)**2)

def rbf_inverse_quadratic(r, epsilon=1.0):
    """Inverse Quadratic: φ(r) = 1/(1 + (εr)²)"""
    return 1.0 / (1 + (epsilon * r)**2)

def rbf_thin_plate_spline(r):
    """Thin Plate Spline: φ(r) = r² log(r)"""
    r_safe = np.maximum(r, 1e-10)  # Avoid log(0)
    return r_safe**2 * np.log(r_safe)

def rbf_linear(r):
    """Linear: φ(r) = r"""
    return r

def rbf_cubic(r):
    """Cubic: φ(r) = r³"""
    return r**3


print("="*70)
print("RADIAL BASIS FUNCTIONS: FUNCTION FAMILY")
print("="*70)

r_vals = np.linspace(0, 3, 300)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(20, 10))
axes = axes.ravel()

rbf_functions = [
    ("Gaussian\nφ(r) = exp(-ε²r²)", rbf_gaussian, {'epsilon': 1.0}),
    ("Multiquadric\nφ(r) = √(1+(εr)²)", rbf_multiquadric, {'epsilon': 1.0}),
    ("Inverse Multiquadric\nφ(r) = 1/√(1+(εr)²)", rbf_inverse_multiquadric, {'epsilon': 1.0}),
    ("Inverse Quadratic\nφ(r) = 1/(1+(εr)²)", rbf_inverse_quadratic, {'epsilon': 1.0}),
    ("Thin Plate Spline\nφ(r) = r²log(r)", rbf_thin_plate_spline, {}),
    ("Linear\nφ(r) = r", rbf_linear, {}),
    ("Cubic\nφ(r) = r³", rbf_cubic, {}),
]

for ax, (name, rbf_fn, params) in zip(axes, rbf_functions):
    y_vals = rbf_fn(r_vals, **params)
    ax.plot(r_vals, y_vals, linewidth=2.5, color='steelblue')
    ax.set_xlabel('Distance r')
    ax.set_ylabel('φ(r)')
    ax.set_title(name)
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    ax.axhline(y=0, color='k', linewidth=0.5)
    ax.axvline(x=0, color='k', linewidth=0.5)

# Summary panel
ax = axes[-1]
ax.text(0.5, 0.5,
        "RBF PROPERTIES:\n\n"
        "Gaussian:\n"
        "• Most common\n"
        "• Smooth, local\n"
        "• Infinitely differentiable\n\n"
        "Multiquadric:\n"
        "• Global influence\n"
        "• Good interpolation\n\n"
        "Thin Plate:\n"
        "• Smoothest interpolant\n"
        "• Used in image warping",
        ha='center', va='center', fontsize=11,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor='wheat', alpha=0.8))
ax.axis('off')

plt.suptitle('Radial Basis Functions: Function Family\n'
             'All depend only on distance r = ||x - c||',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('rbf_function_family.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("Saved: rbf_function_family.png")


# ============================================================
# 2D VISUALIZATION: Radial symmetry

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))

# Create 2D grid
x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 100)

X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)

# Center at origin

R = np.sqrt(X**2 + Y**2)  # Distance from center

rbfs_2d = [

    ("Multiquadric\nε=1", rbf_multiquadric, {'epsilon': 1.0}),

for ax, (name, rbf_fn, params) in zip(axes, rbfs_2d):

docs.title: Mathematical Definition
docs.text:
The RBF kernel (also called Gaussian kernel) is:

K(x, x') = exp(-γ ||x - x'||²)

Where:
  γ (gamma) > 0    is the bandwidth parameter
  ||x - x'||²      is the squared Euclidean distance

Alternative parameterizations:
  K(x, x') = exp(-||x - x'||² / (2σ²))    where γ = 1/(2σ²)
  K(x, x') = exp(-r² / l²)                where γ = 1/l²

docs.title: Why It's Called "RBF Kernel"
docs.text:
RBF Kernel is actually a radial function:

K(x, x') = φ(||x - x'||)    where φ(r) = exp(-γr²)

The value depends ONLY on the distance between x and x'
→ Stationary kernel
→ Translation-invariant
→ Rotation-invariant

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d import Axes3D

# ============================================================
# RBF KERNEL: DETAILED PROPERTIES
# ============================================================

def rbf_kernel(x, xp, gamma=1.0):
    """Standard RBF kernel."""
    diff = x - xp
    return np.exp(-gamma * np.dot(diff, diff))


print("="*70)
print("RBF KERNEL: MATHEMATICAL PROPERTIES")
print("="*70)

# Property 1: Value at identical points
print("\n1. SELF-SIMILARITY")
x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
print(f"   K(x, x) = {rbf_kernel(x, x, gamma=1.0):.6f}")
print(f"   Always equals 1.0 (normalized)")

# Property 2: Decay with distance
print("\n2. DECAY WITH DISTANCE")
x_center = np.array([0.0, 0.0])
distances = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0]

print(f"   {'Distance':<12} {'K(0, x)':<15} {'% of max'}")
print(f"   {'-'*40}")
for d in distances:
    x_test = np.array([d, 0.0])
    k_val  = rbf_kernel(x_center, x_test, gamma=1.0)
    pct    = k_val * 100
    print(f"   {d:<12.1f} {k_val:<15.6f} {pct:>6.1f}%")

print("\n   → Exponential decay: farther points have less influence")

# Property 3: Smoothness
print("\n3. SMOOTHNESS")
print("   RBF kernel is C^∞ (infinitely differentiable)")
print("   → Produces smooth decision boundaries")
print("   → No sharp corners or discontinuities")

# Property 4: Bounded
print("\n4. BOUNDED")
print("   0 < K(x, x') ≤ 1  for all x, x'")
print("   Maximum at x = x' (K = 1)")
print("   Approaches 0 as ||x - x'|| → ∞")

# Property 5: Positive definite
print("\n5. POSITIVE DEFINITE")
print("   RBF kernel is ALWAYS a valid kernel")
print("   → Kernel matrix is always PSD")
print("   → Guaranteed for any γ > 0")


# ============================================================
# VISUALIZE: RBF kernel properties
# ============================================================

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(16, 5))

# Panel 1: Decay curve for different gamma
ax1 = fig.add_subplot(131)
r_vals = np.linspace(0, 4, 200)
gammas = [0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0]

for gamma in gammas:
    k_vals = np.exp(-gamma * r_vals**2)
    ax1.plot(r_vals, k_vals, linewidth=2, label=f'γ={gamma}')

ax1.axhline(y=0.5, color='red', linestyle='--', alpha=0.5,
            label='50% threshold')
ax1.set_xlabel('Distance ||x - x\'||')
ax1.set_ylabel('K(x, x\')')
ax1.set_title('RBF Kernel Decay\nLarger γ → faster decay')
ax1.legend()
ax1.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Panel 2: 2D cross-section
ax2 = fig.add_subplot(132, projection='3d')

x_range = np.linspace(-3, 3, 50)
X_grid, Y_grid = np.meshgrid(x_range, x_range)
Z_grid = np.exp(-1.0 * (X_grid**2 + Y_grid**2))

surf = ax2.plot_surface(X_grid, Y_grid, Z_grid,
                        cmap='viridis', alpha=0.9)
ax2.set_xlabel('x₁ - x\'₁')
ax2.set_ylabel('x₂ - x\'₂')
ax2.set_zlabel('K(x, x\')')
ax2.set_title('RBF Kernel Surface\nγ=1.0')

# Panel 3: Effective range
ax3 = fig.add_subplot(133)

# For different gamma, compute "effective range" (distance where K drops to 0.05)
gammas_range = np.logspace(-1, 1, 50)
effective_ranges = np.sqrt(-np.log(0.05) / gammas_range)

ax3.semilogx(gammas_range, effective_ranges, linewidth=2.5)
ax3.set_xlabel('γ (gamma)')
ax3.set_ylabel('Effective Range\n(distance where K=0.05)')
ax3.set_title('RBF Effective Range vs γ\nLarger γ → smaller range')
ax3.grid(True, alpha=0.3, which='both')
ax3.axhline(y=1.0, color='red', linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)

plt.suptitle('RBF Kernel Properties', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('rbf_kernel_properties.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("\nSaved: rbf_kernel_properties.png")


# ============================================================
# KERNEL MATRIX ANALYSIS
# ============================================================

print("\n" + "="*70)
print("RBF KERNEL MATRIX PROPERTIES")
print("="*70)

np.random.seed(42)
X_rbf = np.random.randn(20, 3)

def rbf_kernel_matrix(X, gamma=1.0):
    n = len(X)
    K = np.zeros((n, n))
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            K[i,j] = rbf_kernel(X[i], X[j], gamma)
    return K

K_rbf = rbf_kernel_matrix(X_rbf, gamma=1.0)

# Analyze
eigvals = np.linalg.eigvalsh(K_rbf)
diag = np.diag(K_rbf)
off_diag = K_rbf[~np.eye(len(X_rbf), dtype=bool)]

print(f"\nKernel matrix shape: {K_rbf.shape}")
print(f"\nDiagonal (self-similarity):")
print(f"  All K(xᵢ,xᵢ) = 1.0: {np.allclose(diag, 1.0)}")
print(f"  Min: {diag.min():.6f}, Max: {diag.max():.6f}")

print(f"\nOff-diagonal (cross-similarity):")
print(f"  Range: [{off_diag.min():.6f}, {off_diag.max():.6f}]")
print(f"  Mean: {off_diag.mean():.6f}")

print(f"\nEigenvalues:")
print(f"  Min: {eigvals.min():.6f}  (> 0 → PSD ✓)")
print(f"  Max: {eigvals.max():.6f}")
print(f"  Condition number: {eigvals.max() / eigvals.min():.2e}")

print(f"\nFrobenius norm: {np.linalg.norm(K_rbf, 'fro'):.4f}")
print(f"Trace (sum of eigenvalues): {np.trace(K_rbf):.4f}")

docs.title: What Gamma Controls
docs.text:
γ (gamma) is the MOST IMPORTANT hyperparameter for RBF kernels

Small γ:
  - Wide Gaussian bell
  - Each training point influences far-away test points
  - Smooth, global decision boundary
  - Risk: UNDERFIT (too simple)

Large γ:
  - Narrow Gaussian bell
  - Each training point influences only nearby test points
  - Complex, local decision boundary
  - Risk: OVERFIT (memorizes training data)

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons, make_circles
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# ============================================================
# GAMMA: COMPLETE SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS
# ============================================================

print("="*70)
print("GAMMA PARAMETER: COMPLETE ANALYSIS")
print("="*70)

np.random.seed(42)
X_gamma, y_gamma = make_moons(n_samples=200, noise=0.2, random_state=42)
X_gamma = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_gamma)

gammas_test = [0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0]

print(f"\n{'γ':<8} {'Train Acc':<12} {'# SV':<8} {'Margin Width*':<15} {'Status'}")
print("-"*60)

results_gamma = []

for gamma in gammas_test:
    clf = SVC(kernel='rbf', gamma=gamma, C=1.0)
    clf.fit(X_gamma, y_gamma)

    train_acc = clf.score(X_gamma, y_gamma) * 100
    n_sv = clf.n_support_.sum()

    # Estimate "effective margin width" from support vector spread
    sv_coords = clf.support_vectors_
    sv_spread = np.std(sv_coords)

    # Classify behavior
    if gamma < 0.1:
        status = "Underfit"
    elif gamma > 5.0:
        status = "Overfit"
    else:
        status = "Good"

    results_gamma.append({
        'gamma': gamma,
        'acc': train_acc,
        'n_sv': n_sv,
        'spread': sv_spread,
        'status': status
    })

    print(f"{gamma:<8.2f} {train_acc:<12.1f} {n_sv:<8} {sv_spread:<15.3f} {status}")


# ============================================================
# VISUALIZE: Effect of gamma on decision boundary
# ============================================================

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(18, 18))
axes = axes.ravel()

for ax, gamma in zip(axes, gammas_test):
    clf = SVC(kernel='rbf', gamma=gamma, C=1.0)
    clf.fit(X_gamma, y_gamma)

    # Create mesh
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(
        np.linspace(X_gamma[:,0].min()-0.5, X_gamma[:,0].max()+0.5, 200),
        np.linspace(X_gamma[:,1].min()-0.5, X_gamma[:,1].max()+0.5, 200)
    )

    Z = clf.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).reshape(xx.shape)

    # Plot
    ax.contourf(xx, yy, Z, alpha=0.25, cmap='RdYlBu')
    ax.contour(xx, yy, Z, colors='k', linewidths=1, alpha=0.5)

    ax.scatter(X_gamma[y_gamma==0, 0], X_gamma[y_gamma==0, 1],
               c='royalblue', s=25, edgecolors='k', linewidths=0.3, alpha=0.8)
    ax.scatter(X_gamma[y_gamma==1, 0], X_gamma[y_gamma==1, 1],
               c='tomato', s=25, marker='s',
               edgecolors='k', linewidths=0.3, alpha=0.8)

    # Highlight support vectors
    sv = clf.support_vectors_
    ax.scatter(sv[:,0], sv[:,1], s=150, facecolors='none',
               edgecolors='gold', linewidths=2.5, zorder=5)

    acc = clf.score(X_gamma, y_gamma) * 100
    n_sv = clf.n_support_.sum()

    ax.set_title(f'γ = {gamma}\nAcc={acc:.0f}%, SV={n_sv}')
    ax.set_xlim(X_gamma[:,0].min()-0.5, X_gamma[:,0].max()+0.5)
    ax.set_ylim(X_gamma[:,1].min()-0.5, X_gamma[:,1].max()+0.5)
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.suptitle('Effect of γ on RBF-SVM Decision Boundary\n'
             'Top-left (small γ) = smooth, global → Bottom-right (large γ) = complex, local',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('gamma_sensitivity.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("\nSaved: gamma_sensitivity.png")


# ============================================================
# GAMMA vs ACCURACY: LEARNING CURVE
# ============================================================

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
    X_gamma, y_gamma, test_size=0.3, random_state=42
)

gammas_fine = np.logspace(-2, 2, 50)
train_accs = []
test_accs = []
n_svs = []

for gamma in gammas_fine:
    clf = SVC(kernel='rbf', gamma=gamma, C=1.0)
    clf.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    train_accs.append(clf.score(X_tr, y_tr))
    test_accs.append(clf.score(X_te, y_te))
    n_svs.append(clf.n_support_.sum())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

# Accuracy vs gamma
ax = axes[0]
ax.semilogx(gammas_fine, train_accs, 'b-', linewidth=2.5, label='Train')
ax.semilogx(gammas_fine, test_accs, 'r--', linewidth=2.5, label='Test')
ax.set_xlabel('γ (gamma)', fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel('Accuracy', fontsize=12)
ax.set_title('Accuracy vs γ\n(Underfit ← optimal → Overfit)')
ax.legend(fontsize=11)
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3, which='both')
ax.axvline(x=gammas_fine[np.argmax(test_accs)],
           color='green', linestyle=':', linewidth=2,
           label=f'Best γ = {gammas_fine[np.argmax(test_accs)]:.3f}')

# Number of support vectors vs gamma
ax = axes[1]
ax.semilogx(gammas_fine, n_svs, 'purple', linewidth=2.5)
ax.set_xlabel('γ (gamma)', fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel('# Support Vectors', fontsize=12)
ax.set_title('Support Vectors vs γ\nMore SV = simpler model (less overfitting)')
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3, which='both')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('gamma_learning_curve.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("Saved: gamma_learning_curve.png")

print(f"\nOptimal γ: {gammas_fine[np.argmax(test_accs)]:.4f}")
print(f"Best test accuracy: {max(test_accs)*100:.2f}%")

# ============================================================
# GAMMA: THREE INTERPRETATIONS
# ============================================================

print("\n" + "="*70)
print("GAMMA: THREE EQUIVALENT INTERPRETATIONS")
print("="*70)

gamma_val = 1.0

# Interpretation 1: Bandwidth
sigma = 1 / np.sqrt(2 * gamma_val)
print(f"\n1. BANDWIDTH PARAMETER")
print(f"   γ = {gamma_val}")
print(f"   K(x,x') = exp(-γ||x-x'||²)")
print(f"   Equivalent σ = 1/√(2γ) = {sigma:.4f}")
print(f"   → Gaussian with standard deviation σ")

# Interpretation 2: Length scale
length_scale = 1 / np.sqrt(gamma_val)
print(f"\n2. LENGTH SCALE")
print(f"   l = 1/√γ = {length_scale:.4f}")
print(f"   K(x,x') = exp(-||x-x'||²/l²)")
print(f"   → Points farther than l have low correlation")

# Interpretation 3: Inverse reach
print(f"\n3. INVERSE REACH")
print(f"   γ controls how far influence extends:")

distances_test = np.array([0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0])
print(f"\n   {'Distance':<12} {'K(x,x\')':<15} {'Influence'}")
print(f"   {'-'*45}")
for d in distances_test:
    k_val = np.exp(-gamma_val * d**2)
    influence = "Strong" if k_val > 0.5 else "Moderate" if k_val > 0.1 else "Weak"
    print(f"   {d:<12.1f} {k_val:<15.4f} {influence}")

print(f"\n   Effective radius (K > 0.05): {np.sqrt(-np.log(0.05)/gamma_val):.3f}")

from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification, make_moons, make_circles
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

import time

# ============================================================
# RBF VS OTHER KERNELS: COMPREHENSIVE COMPARISON
# ============================================================

print("="*70)
print("RBF VS OTHER KERNELS")
print("="*70)

datasets_comp = {
    'Linear Sep': make_classification(n_samples=200, n_features=2,
                                      n_redundant=0, n_informative=2,
                                      class_sep=2.5, random_state=42),
    'Moons': make_moons(n_samples=200, noise=0.2, random_state=42),
    'Circles': make_circles(n_samples=200, noise=0.1,
                            factor=0.4, random_state=42),
}

kernels_comp = {
    'Linear':    SVC(kernel='linear', C=1.0),
    'Poly d=2':  SVC(kernel='poly', degree=2, coef0=1, C=1.0),
    'Poly d=3':  SVC(kernel='poly', degree=3, coef0=1, C=1.0),
    'RBF γ=auto': SVC(kernel='rbf', gamma='auto', C=1.0),
    'RBF γ=scale': SVC(kernel='rbf', gamma='scale', C=1.0),
    'Sigmoid':   SVC(kernel='sigmoid', gamma=0.1, coef0=0, C=1.0),
}

print(f"\n{'Dataset':<15} {'Kernel':<15} {'CV Acc':<12} {'Train Time':<12} {'# SV'}")
print("-"*65)

results_comp = {}

for ds_name, (X_ds, y_ds) in datasets_comp.items():
    X_s = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_ds)
    results_comp[ds_name] = {}

    for k_name, clf in kernels_comp.items():
        # Cross-validation score
        scores = cross_val_score(clf, X_s, y_ds, cv=5)
        mean_score = scores.mean()

        # Training time
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        clf.fit(X_s, y_ds)
        train_time = time.perf_counter() - t0

        n_sv = clf.n_support_.sum() if hasattr(clf, 'n_support_') else 0

        results_comp[ds_name][k_name] = {
            'cv_acc': mean_score,
            'time': train_time,
            'n_sv': n_sv
        }

        print(f"{ds_name:<15} {k_name:<15} {mean_score*100:<12.1f} "
              f"{train_time*1000:<12.2f} {n_sv}")


# ============================================================
# SUMMARY: When RBF wins
# ============================================================

print("\n" + "="*70)
print("WHEN RBF KERNEL WINS")
print("="*70)

summary = """
RBF is the BEST choice when:
  ✓ Data has non-linear patterns (moons, circles, spirals)
  ✓ No prior knowledge about data structure
  ✓ Need universal approximation capability
  ✓ Want smooth, continuous boundaries
  ✓ Can afford to tune gamma via cross-validation

RBF may NOT be the best when:
  ✗ Data is linearly separable (linear kernel faster + simpler)
  ✗ Very high-dimensional text data (linear often better)
  ✗ Need polynomial interactions specifically (use poly kernel)
  ✗ Very large datasets (>100K samples, RBF becomes slow)

RULE OF THUMB:
  Start with RBF (gamma='scale'), tune if needed
  Try linear kernel as baseline
  If RBF doesn't improve much → use linear (simpler)
"""

print(summary)


# ============================================================

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 4, figsize=(20, 15))

for row, (ds_name, (X_ds, y_ds)) in enumerate(datasets_comp.items()):

        Z = clf.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).reshape(xx.shape)

                   s=20, edgecolors='k', linewidths=0.3)
        ax.scatter(X_s[y_ds==1,0], X_s[y_ds==1,1], c='tomato',
                   s=20, marker='s', edgecolors='k', linewidths=0.3)

        acc = clf.score(X_s, y_ds) * 100

plt.suptitle('RBF vs Other Kernels: Decision Boundaries\n'
             'RBF excels on non-linear patterns',

docs.title: What Is an RBF Network?
docs.text:
An RBF Network is a neural network architecture that uses radial basis functions as activation functions:

RBF Network Structure:

Input x → Hidden Layer (RBF neurons) → Output Layer (linear)
          φ₁(||x - c₁||)
          φ₂(||x - c₂||)              Σ wᵢφᵢ + b
          ...                    →
          φₖ(||x - cₖ||)

Where:
  cᵢ = center of RBF neuron i
  φᵢ = RBF activation (typically Gaussian)
  wᵢ = output weight

Output: f(x) = Σᵢ wᵢ exp(-γ||x - cᵢ||²) + b

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

# ============================================================
# RBF NETWORK: FROM SCRATCH
# ============================================================

class RBFNetwork:
    """
    Radial Basis Function Network for regression/classification.

    Architecture:
      Input → RBF hidden layer → Linear output
    """

    def __init__(self, n_centers=10, gamma=1.0):
        self.n_centers = n_centers
        self.gamma = gamma
        self.centers = None
        self.weights = None
        self.bias = 0.0

    def _rbf_activation(self, X, center):
        """Compute RBF activation: exp(-γ||x - c||²)"""
        distances_sq = np.sum((X - center)**2, axis=1)
        return np.exp(-self.gamma * distances_sq)

    def _compute_activations(self, X):
        """Compute activations for all RBF neurons."""
        n = len(X)
        activations = np.zeros((n, self.n_centers))
        for i, center in enumerate(self.centers):
            activations[:, i] = self._rbf_activation(X, center)
        return activations

    def fit(self, X, y, center_method='kmeans'):
        """
        Train RBF network.

        Step 1: Choose centers (k-means or random)
        Step 2: Compute RBF activations
        Step 3: Solve for output weights (linear least squares)
        """
        if center_method == 'kmeans':
            # Use k-means to find centers
            kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=self.n_centers, random_state=42)
            kmeans.fit(X)
            self.centers = kmeans.cluster_centers_
        elif center_method == 'random':
            # Random subset of training points
            indices = np.random.choice(len(X), self.n_centers, replace=False)
            self.centers = X[indices]
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown center_method: {center_method}")

        # Compute activations
        H = self._compute_activations(X)

        # Solve for weights: y = Hw + b
        # Add bias column
        H_bias = np.column_stack([H, np.ones(len(X))])

        # Least squares
        w_full = np.linalg.lstsq(H_bias, y, rcond=None)[0]
        self.weights = w_full[:-1]
        self.bias = w_full[-1]

        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        """Predict using trained RBF network."""
        H = self._compute_activations(X)
        return H @ self.weights + self.bias

    def score(self, X, y):
        """R² score for regression."""
        y_pred = self.predict(X)
        ss_res = np.sum((y - y_pred)**2)
        ss_tot = np.sum((y - y.mean())**2)
        return 1 - ss_res / (ss_tot + 1e-10)


print("="*70)
print("RBF NETWORK: DEMONSTRATION")
print("="*70)

# Generate non-linear regression data
np.random.seed(42)
n_samples = 200
X_rbfn = np.sort(np.random.uniform(0, 10, n_samples)).reshape(-1, 1)
y_rbfn = np.sin(X_rbfn.ravel()) + 0.3*np.sin(3*X_rbfn.ravel()) + \
         np.random.randn(n_samples) * 0.2

X_test_rbfn = np.linspace(0, 10, 300).reshape(-1, 1)
y_true_rbfn = np.sin(X_test_rbfn.ravel()) + 0.3*np.sin(3*X_test_rbfn.ravel())

# Train RBF networks with different number of centers
n_centers_list = [5, 10, 20, 40]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 10))
axes = axes.ravel()

for ax, n_centers in zip(axes, n_centers_list):
    rbfn = RBFNetwork(n_centers=n_centers, gamma=1.0)
    rbfn.fit(X_rbfn, y_rbfn, center_method='kmeans')

    y_pred = rbfn.predict(X_test_rbfn)
    r2 = rbfn.score(X_rbfn, y_rbfn)

    ax.scatter(X_rbfn, y_rbfn, c='gray', s=10, alpha=0.5, label='Data')
    ax.plot(X_test_rbfn, y_true_rbfn, 'g-', linewidth=2, label='True')
    ax.plot(X_test_rbfn, y_pred, 'r--', linewidth=2, label='RBF Network')

    # Plot centers
    ax.scatter(rbfn.centers, np.zeros(len(rbfn.centers)),
               c='blue', s=100, marker='^', zorder=5,
               label=f'Centers ({n_centers})')

    ax.set_xlabel('x')
    ax.set_ylabel('y')
    ax.set_title(f'RBF Network: {n_centers} centers\nR² = {r2:.3f}')
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.suptitle('RBF Network: Effect of Number of Centers\n'
             'More centers = more capacity',
             fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('rbf_network.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("Saved: rbf_network.png")

print(f"\nRBF Network trained with {n_centers_list[-1]} centers:")
print(f"  Training R²: {rbfn.score(X_rbfn, y_rbfn):.4f}")


# ============================================================
# RBF NETWORK vs KERNEL RIDGE REGRESSION
# ============================================================

from sklearn.kernel_ridge import KernelRidge

print("\n" + "="*70)
print("RBF NETWORK vs KERNEL RIDGE REGRESSION")
print("="*70)

# Train both
rbfn_comp = RBFNetwork(n_centers=20, gamma=1.0)
rbfn_comp.fit(X_rbfn, y_rbfn)

kr = KernelRidge(kernel='rbf', alpha=0.01, gamma=1.0)
kr.fit(X_rbfn, y_rbfn)

# Compare
y_rbfn_pred = rbfn_comp.predict(X_test_rbfn)
y_kr_pred = kr.predict(X_test_rbfn)

mse_rbfn = np.mean((y_rbfn_pred - y_true_rbfn)**2)
mse_kr = np.mean((y_kr_pred - y_true_rbfn)**2)

print(f"\nRBF Network (20 centers):")
print(f"  MSE: {mse_rbfn:.4f}")
print(f"  Parameters: {n_centers * 1 + n_centers} (centers + weights)")

print(f"\nKernel Ridge Regression:")
print(f"  MSE: {mse_kr:.4f}")
print(f"  Parameters: {len(X_rbfn)} (one per training point)")

print(f"\nDifference:")
print(f"  RBF Network is {len(X_rbfn) / n_centers:.1f}x more compact")
print(f"  But Kernel Ridge is typically more accurate")

from sklearn.gaussian_process import GaussianProcessRegressor
from sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels import RBF, ConstantKernel as C

# ============================================================
# GAUSSIAN PROCESS with RBF KERNEL
# ============================================================

print("="*70)
print("GAUSSIAN PROCESS REGRESSION with RBF")
print("="*70)

np.random.seed(42)
n_gp = 30
X_gp = np.sort(np.random.uniform(0, 10, n_gp)).reshape(-1, 1)
y_gp = np.sin(X_gp.ravel()) + np.random.randn(n_gp) * 0.2

X_test_gp = np.linspace(0, 10, 300).reshape(-1, 1)
y_true_gp = np.sin(X_test_gp.ravel())

# Define GP with RBF kernel
kernel = C(1.0) * RBF(length_scale=1.0)
gp = GaussianProcessRegressor(kernel=kernel, alpha=0.1, n_restarts_optimizer=10)

print(f"\nKernel: {kernel}")

# Fit
gp.fit(X_gp, y_gp)

print(f"\nOptimized kernel: {gp.kernel_}")
print(f"Log marginal likelihood: {gp.log_marginal_likelihood(gp.kernel_.theta):.4f}")

# Predict with uncertainty
y_pred_gp, sigma = gp.predict(X_test_gp, return_std=True)

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

# Panel 1: Predictions with uncertainty
ax = axes[0]
ax.scatter(X_gp, y_gp, c='red', s=50, zorder=10, label='Training data')
ax.plot(X_test_gp, y_true_gp, 'g--', linewidth=1.5, alpha=0.7, label='True function')
ax.plot(X_test_gp, y_pred_gp, 'b-', linewidth=2, label='GP mean')
ax.fill_between(X_test_gp.ravel(),
                y_pred_gp - 1.96*sigma,
                y_pred_gp + 1.96*sigma,
                alpha=0.2, color='blue', label='95% confidence')
ax.set_xlabel('x')
ax.set_ylabel('y')
ax.set_title('Gaussian Process with RBF Kernel\n(Prediction + Uncertainty)')
ax.legend()
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Panel 2: Uncertainty alone
ax = axes[1]
ax.plot(X_test_gp, sigma, 'purple', linewidth=2.5)
for x_train in X_gp:
    ax.axvline(x=x_train, color='red', alpha=0.3, linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel('x')
ax.set_ylabel('Uncertainty (σ)')
ax.set_title('Predictive Uncertainty\n(High where no training data)')
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.suptitle('Gaussian Process with RBF Kernel',
             fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('gp_rbf.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("\nSaved: gp_rbf.png")

print("\nKey observations:")
print("  - GP provides uncertainty estimates (not just point predictions)")
print("  - Uncertainty is LOW near training data, HIGH far from it")
print("  - RBF kernel controls smoothness via length_scale parameter")

print("\n" + "="*70)
print("GAMMA SELECTION: GRID SEARCH")
print("="*70)

X_grid, y_grid = make_classification(
    n_samples=300, n_features=10, n_informative=8,
    n_redundant=2, random_state=42
)
X_grid = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_grid)

# Define grid
param_grid = {
    'C': [0.1, 1, 10, 100],
    'gamma': [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 'scale', 'auto']
}

# Grid search
clf_grid = GridSearchCV(
    SVC(kernel='rbf'),
    param_grid,
    cv=5,
    scoring='accuracy',
    n_jobs=-1
)

clf_grid.fit(X_grid, y_grid)

print(f"\nBest parameters: {clf_grid.best_params_}")
print(f"Best CV score: {clf_grid.best_score_*100:.2f}%")

# Show top 5
results_df = clf_grid.cv_results_
indices = np.argsort(results_df['mean_test_score'])[::-1][:5]

print(f"\nTop 5 parameter combinations:")
print(f"{'Rank':<6} {'C':<10} {'gamma':<12} {'Mean CV Acc'}")
print("-"*42)
for rank, idx in enumerate(indices, 1):
    c = results_df['param_C'][idx]
    g = results_df['param_gamma'][idx]
    acc = results_df['mean_test_score'][idx]
    print(f"{rank:<6} {c:<10} {str(g):<12} {acc*100:.2f}%")

docs.title: Strategy 3: Median Heuristic
docs.text:
from sklearn.metrics import pairwise_distances

# ============================================================
# MEDIAN HEURISTIC for GAMMA
# ============================================================

print("\n" + "="*70)
print("GAMMA SELECTION: MEDIAN HEURISTIC")
print("="*70)

def median_heuristic_gamma(X):
    """
    Median heuristic: set γ = 1 / (2 × median²(pairwise distances))

    Rationale: median distance is a robust estimate of typical scale
    """
    # Compute pairwise distances
    dists = pairwise_distances(X)

    # Get upper triangle (exclude diagonal and duplicates)
    n = len(X)
    triu_indices = np.triu_indices(n, k=1)
    dists_upper = dists[triu_indices]

    # Median distance
    median_dist = np.median(dists_upper)

    # Gamma
    gamma = 1.0 / (2 * median_dist**2)

    return gamma, median_dist


X_median = np.random.randn(100, 3)

gamma_median, med_dist = median_heuristic_gamma(X_median)
gamma_scale = 1.0 / (X_median.shape[1] * X_median.var())
gamma_auto = 1.0 / X_median.shape[1]

print(f"\nThree gamma strategies:")
print(f"  Median heuristic: γ = {gamma_median:.6f}  (median dist = {med_dist:.4f})")
print(f"  sklearn 'scale':  γ = {gamma_scale:.6f}")
print(f"  sklearn 'auto':   γ = {gamma_auto:.6f}")

print(f"\nMedian heuristic is useful when:")
print(f"  - Data has been standardized")
print(f"  - You want a data-driven default")
print(f"  - Grid search is too expensive")

# ============================================================
# GAMMA SELECTION: LEARNING CURVES
# ============================================================

from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve

print("\n" + "="*70)
print("GAMMA SELECTION: LEARNING CURVES")
print("="*70)

X_lc, y_lc = make_classification(
    n_samples=500, n_features=10, n_informative=8,
    random_state=42
)
X_lc = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_lc)

gammas_lc = [0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10))
axes = axes.ravel()

for ax, gamma in zip(axes, gammas_lc):
    train_sizes, train_scores, test_scores = learning_curve(
        SVC(kernel='rbf', gamma=gamma, C=1.0),
        X_lc, y_lc,
        train_sizes=np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 10),
        cv=5,
        n_jobs=-1
    )

    train_mean = train_scores.mean(axis=1)
    train_std = train_scores.std(axis=1)
    test_mean = test_scores.mean(axis=1)
    test_std = test_scores.std(axis=1)

    ax.plot(train_sizes, train_mean, 'o-', linewidth=2, label='Training')
    ax.fill_between(train_sizes, train_mean - train_std,
                    train_mean + train_std, alpha=0.2)

    ax.plot(train_sizes, test_mean, 's-', linewidth=2, label='Validation')
    ax.fill_between(train_sizes, test_mean - test_std,
                    test_mean + test_std, alpha=0.2)

    ax.set_xlabel('Training Set Size')
    ax.set_ylabel('Accuracy')
    ax.set_title(f'γ = {gamma}')
    ax.legend()
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    ax.set_ylim([0.5, 1.05])

plt.suptitle('Learning Curves for Different γ\n'
             'Look for: high validation acc, small train-val gap',
             fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('gamma_learning_curves.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("Saved: gamma_learning_curves.png")

print("  - Both low: UNDERFITTING → increase γ")
print("  - Both high, small gap: GOOD FIT ✓")

# ============================================================
# RBF INTERPOLATION
# ============================================================

print("="*70)
print("RBF INTERPOLATION")
print("="*70)

from scipy.interpolate import Rbf

# Generate scattered data
np.random.seed(42)
n_interp = 20
X_interp = np.random.uniform(-5, 5, n_interp)
Y_interp = np.random.uniform(-5, 5, n_interp)
Z_interp = np.sin(np.sqrt(X_interp**2 + Y_interp**2))

# Create RBF interpolator
rbf_interp = Rbf(X_interp, Y_interp, Z_interp, function='gaussian', epsilon=2)

# Evaluate on grid
xi = np.linspace(-5, 5, 100)
yi = np.linspace(-5, 5, 100)
XI, YI = np.meshgrid(xi, yi)
ZI = rbf_interp(XI, YI)

# True function
Z_true = np.sin(np.sqrt(XI**2 + YI**2))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))

# Scattered data
ax = axes[0]
scatter = ax.scatter(X_interp, Y_interp, c=Z_interp,
                     s=100, cmap='viridis', edgecolors='k', linewidths=1.5)
ax.set_xlabel('x')
ax.set_ylabel('y')
ax.set_title('Scattered Data Points\n(20 samples)')
plt.colorbar(scatter, ax=ax)
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# RBF interpolation
ax = axes[1]
cf = ax.contourf(XI, YI, ZI, levels=20, cmap='viridis')
ax.scatter(X_interp, Y_interp, c='red', s=30, marker='x', linewidths=2)
ax.set_xlabel('x')
ax.set_ylabel('y')
ax.set_title('RBF Interpolation\n(Smooth reconstruction)')
plt.colorbar(cf, ax=ax)

# True function
ax = axes[2]
cf = ax.contourf(XI, YI, Z_true, levels=20, cmap='viridis')
ax.scatter(X_interp, Y_interp, c='red', s=30, marker='x', linewidths=2)
ax.set_xlabel('x')
ax.set_ylabel('y')
ax.set_title('True Function\nsin(√(x²+y²))')
plt.colorbar(cf, ax=ax)

plt.suptitle('RBF Interpolation for Scattered Data',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('rbf_interpolation.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("Saved: rbf_interpolation.png")

# Error
error = np.abs(ZI - Z_true)
print(f"\nInterpolation error:")
print(f"  Mean absolute error: {error.mean():.4f}")
print(f"  Max absolute error: {error.max():.4f}")

docs.title: Time Complexity
docs.text:
Training:
  - Kernel matrix computation: O(n² × d)
  - QP solving: O(n² × n_sv) to O(n³)
  - Total: O(n²d) to O(n³)

Prediction (single point):
  - Compute K(x, xᵢ) for all support vectors: O(n_sv × d)

Memory:
  - Kernel matrix: O(n²)  (can be HUGE!)
  - Support vectors: O(n_sv × d)

import time
import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# ============================================================
# COMPUTATIONAL COMPLEXITY: EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS
# ============================================================

print("="*70)
print("RBF KERNEL: COMPUTATIONAL COMPLEXITY")
print("="*70)

sizes = [100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000]
dimensions = [5, 10, 20]

print(f"\n{'n':<8} {'d':<8} {'Train Time (s)':<18} {'Predict Time (ms)':<20} {'# SV'}")
print("-"*70)

for n in sizes:
    for d in dimensions:
        if n * d > 50000:  # Skip very large cases
            continue

        X = np.random.randn(n, d)
        y = (X.sum(axis=1) > 0).astype(int)
        X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

        X_train, X_test = X[:int(0.8*n)], X[int(0.8*n):]
        y_train, y_test = y[:int(0.8*n)], y[int(0.8*n):]

        # Train
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        clf = SVC(kernel='rbf', gamma='scale', C=1.0)
        clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
        train_time = time.perf_counter() - t0

        # Predict
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        _ = clf.predict(X_test)
        predict_time = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / len(X_test) * 1000

        n_sv = clf.n_support_.sum()

        print(f"{n:<8} {d:<8} {train_time:<18.4f} {predict_time:<20.2f} {n_sv}")


# ============================================================
# SCALING: Visualize complexity
# ============================================================

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

# Theoretical complexity
n_vals = np.logspace(2, 4, 50)

ax = axes[0]
ax.loglog(n_vals, n_vals**2 * 5, label='O(n²) — Kernel matrix', linewidth=2.5)
ax.loglog(n_vals, n_vals**3 / 1000, label='O(n³) — QP solving', linewidth=2.5)
ax.set_xlabel('Dataset Size (n)')
ax.set_ylabel('Operations')
ax.set_title('Training Time Complexity')
ax.legend()
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3, which='both')

# Memory complexity
ax = axes[1]
ax.loglog(n_vals, n_vals**2 * 8 / 1e9, linewidth=2.5, color='purple')
ax.set_xlabel('Dataset Size (n)')
ax.set_ylabel('Memory (GB)')
ax.set_title('Memory Complexity\n(Kernel matrix: n² doubles)')
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3, which='both')
ax.axhline(y=8, color='red', linestyle='--', label='8 GB RAM')
ax.axhline(y=32, color='orange', linestyle='--', label='32 GB RAM')
ax.legend()

plt.suptitle('RBF-SVM Computational Complexity',
             fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('rbf_complexity.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("\nSaved: rbf_complexity.png")

print("\nPractical limits:")
print("  n < 10,000:   Fast, practical")
print("  n = 10-100K:  Slow but feasible with patience")
print("  n > 100K:     Impractical for standard RBF-SVM")
print("                → Use linear SVM or approximate kernels")

from sklearn.kernel_approximation import RBFSampler, Nystroem

# ============================================================
# KERNEL APPROXIMATION for LARGE DATASETS
# ============================================================

print("\n" + "="*70)
print("KERNEL APPROXIMATION METHODS")
print("="*70)

# Large dataset
n_large = 10000
X_large = np.random.randn(n_large, 20)
y_large = (X_large.sum(axis=1) > 0).astype(int)
X_large = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_large)

X_tr_l, X_te_l = X_large[:8000], X_large[8000:]
y_tr_l, y_te_l = y_large[:8000], y_large[8000:]

print(f"\nDataset size: {n_large} samples, 20 features")

# Method 1: Random Fourier Features (RFF)
print("\n1. RANDOM FOURIER FEATURES (Rahimi & Recht, 2007)")
rbf_sampler = RBFSampler(gamma=1.0, n_components=100, random_state=42)
X_tr_rff = rbf_sampler.fit_transform(X_tr_l)
X_te_rff = rbf_sampler.transform(X_te_l)

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
clf_rff = LogisticRegression()

t0 = time.perf_counter()
clf_rff.fit(X_tr_rff, y_tr_l)
time_rff = time.perf_counter() - t0

acc_rff = clf_rff.score(X_te_rff, y_te_l)

print(f"  Explicit features: {X_tr_rff.shape[1]}")
print(f"  Training time: {time_rff:.4f}s")
print(f"  Test accuracy: {acc_rff*100:.2f}%")

# Method 2: Nyström approximation
print("\n2. NYSTRÖM APPROXIMATION")
nystroem = Nystroem(kernel='rbf', gamma=1.0, n_components=100, random_state=42)
X_tr_nys = nystroem.fit_transform(X_tr_l)
X_te_nys = nystroem.transform(X_te_l)

clf_nys = LogisticRegression()

t0 = time.perf_counter()
clf_nys.fit(X_tr_nys, y_tr_l)
time_nys = time.perf_counter() - t0

acc_nys = clf_nys.score(X_te_nys, y_te_l)

print(f"  Explicit features: {X_tr_nys.shape[1]}")
print(f"  Training time: {time_nys:.4f}s")
print(f"  Test accuracy: {acc_nys*100:.2f}%")

# Method 3: Exact kernel (too slow for large data, but shown for comparison on subset)
print("\n3. EXACT RBF KERNEL (on 1000-sample subset)")
X_tr_sub = X_tr_l[:1000]
y_tr_sub = y_tr_l[:1000]

clf_exact = SVC(kernel='rbf', gamma=1.0, C=1.0)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
clf_exact.fit(X_tr_sub, y_tr_sub)
time_exact = time.perf_counter() - t0

acc_exact = clf_exact.score(X_te_l, y_te_l)

print(f"  Training size: {len(X_tr_sub)}")
print(f"  Training time: {time_exact:.4f}s")
print(f"  Test accuracy: {acc_exact*100:.2f}%")

print("\n" + "="*70)
print("SUMMARY")
print("="*70)
print(f"{'Method':<25} {'Train Time':<15} {'Accuracy':<12} {'Speedup'}")
print("-"*65)
print(f"{'Random Fourier Features':<25} {time_rff:<15.4f} {acc_rff*100:<12.2f} {time_exact/time_rff:.1f}x")
print(f"{'Nyström':<25} {time_nys:<15.4f} {acc_nys*100:<12.2f} {time_exact/time_nys:.1f}x")
print(f"{'Exact (subset)':<25} {time_exact:<15.4f} {acc_exact*100:<12.2f} 1.0x")

print("\nFor large datasets (n > 10K):")
print("  → Use kernel approximation methods")
print("  → Or switch to linear models")

docs.title: RBF Kernel: Complete Summary
docs.text:
print("="*70)
print("RBF KERNEL: COMPLETE SUMMARY")
print("="*70)

summary_text = """
DEFINITION:
  K(x, x') = exp(-γ ||x - x'||²)

WHY RBF IS POPULAR:
  ✓ Universal approximator (can fit any continuous function)
  ✓ Always valid (PSD for any γ > 0)
  ✓ Smooth, infinitely differentiable
  ✓ Stationary (translation-invariant)
  ✓ Single hyperparameter (γ) to tune
  ✓ Works well as default choice

GAMMA CONTROLS:
  Small γ → Wide influence, smooth boundaries, underfit risk
  Large γ → Narrow influence, complex boundaries, overfit risk

GAMMA SELECTION STRATEGIES:
  1. gamma='scale' (sklearn default): 1/(d × var(X))
  2. Grid search with CV
  3. Median heuristic: 1/(2 × median²(distances))
  4. Learning curves

WHEN TO USE RBF:
  ✓ Non-linear patterns
  ✓ No prior knowledge of data structure
  ✓ Small-to-medium datasets (n < 10K)
  ✓ Need smooth boundaries

WHEN NOT TO USE RBF:
  ✗ Linearly separable data (use linear kernel)
  ✗ Very large datasets (n > 100K) → too slow
  ✗ High-dimensional sparse data (text) → linear often better

COMPUTATIONAL COST:
  Training: O(n²d) to O(n³)
  Memory: O(n²) for kernel matrix
  Prediction: O(n_sv × d) per point

ALTERNATIVES FOR LARGE DATA:
  - Random Fourier Features
  - Nyström approximation
  - Linear models
"""

print(summary_text)

docs.title: The Core Idea
docs.text:
Given linearly separable data, there are infinitely many hyperplanes that can separate the classes. Which one should we choose?

SVM's answer: Choose the hyperplane with the maximum margin — the largest minimum distance to any training point.

Why maximum margin?

1. GENERALIZATION: Larger margin → better generalization
2. ROBUSTNESS: Farther from noise and perturbations  
3. UNIQUENESS: Only one maximum-margin hyperplane exists
4. GEOMETRIC: Natural notion of "best" separation

docs.title: Visual Intuition
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Generate linearly separable data
np.random.seed(42)
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=100, n_features=2, n_redundant=0,
                           n_informative=2, class_sep=2.5, random_state=42)
y = np.where(y == 0, -1, 1)
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

# Train SVM
svm = SVC(kernel='linear', C=1e6)  # Large C ≈ hard margin
svm.fit(X, y)

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

# Panel 1: Multiple separating hyperplanes
ax = axes[0]
ax.scatter(X[y==-1, 0], X[y==-1, 1], c='blue', s=50, label='Class -1')
ax.scatter(X[y==1, 0], X[y==1, 1], c='red', s=50, marker='s', label='Class +1')

# Draw several possible separating lines
for slope, intercept in [(0.5, 0.2), (0.7, -0.1), (0.9, 0.3), (1.1, 0.0)]:
    x_line = np.linspace(-3, 3, 100)
    y_line = slope * x_line + intercept
    ax.plot(x_line, y_line, 'k--', alpha=0.3, linewidth=1)

ax.text(0, 2, 'Many possible\nseparating hyperplanes', fontsize=11,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor='yellow', alpha=0.7))
ax.set_xlim(-3, 3); ax.set_ylim(-3, 3)
ax.legend(); ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
ax.set_title('Infinite Separating Hyperplanes')

# Panel 2: Maximum margin hyperplane
ax = axes[1]
w = svm.coef_[0]
b = svm.intercept_[0]

xx = np.linspace(-3, 3, 100)
yy_boundary = -(w[0] * xx + b) / w[1]
yy_margin_pos = -(w[0] * xx + b - 1) / w[1]
yy_margin_neg = -(w[0] * xx + b + 1) / w[1]

ax.plot(xx, yy_boundary, 'k-', linewidth=2, label='Decision boundary')
ax.plot(xx, yy_margin_pos, 'r--', linewidth=1.5, label='Margin +1')
ax.plot(xx, yy_margin_neg, 'b--', linewidth=1.5, label='Margin -1')

ax.scatter(X[y==-1, 0], X[y==-1, 1], c='blue', s=50)
ax.scatter(X[y==1, 0], X[y==1, 1], c='red', s=50, marker='s')

# Highlight support vectors
sv = svm.support_vectors_
ax.scatter(sv[:, 0], sv[:, 1], s=200, facecolors='none',
           edgecolors='gold', linewidths=3, label='Support Vectors')

margin_width = 2 / np.linalg.norm(w)
ax.text(0, 2, f'Maximum margin\nwidth = {margin_width:.3f}', fontsize=11,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor='lightgreen', alpha=0.7))

ax.set_xlim(-3, 3); ax.set_ylim(-3, 3)
ax.legend(); ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
ax.set_title('SVM: Maximum Margin Hyperplane')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('hard_margin_principle.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("Saved: hard_margin_principle.png")

docs.title: The Decision Boundary
docs.text:
A hyperplane in ℝᵈ is defined by:

wᵀx + b = 0

Where:
  w ∈ ℝᵈ  is the weight vector (normal to the hyperplane)
  b ∈ ℝ   is the bias term
  x ∈ ℝᵈ  is any point on the hyperplane

docs.title: Distance from Point to Hyperplane
docs.text:
The signed distance from a point x to the hyperplane wᵀx + b = 0 is:

distance = (wᵀx + b) / ||w||

Where ||w|| = √(w₁² + w₂² + ... + wₐ²)

Sign indicates which side of the hyperplane:
  > 0:  point is on the +1 side
  < 0:  point is on the -1 side

docs.title: Margin Definition
docs.text:
The margin is the perpendicular distance from the decision boundary to the nearest data point.

For correctly classified points:
  yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) > 0    (correct side)

Functional margin:  yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b)
Geometric margin:   yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) / ||w||

The margin of the classifier is:
  γ = min_{i=1,...,n} yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) / ||w||

# Verify margin calculation
print("="*60)
print("MARGIN CALCULATION")
print("="*60)

w = svm.coef_[0]
b = svm.intercept_[0]
w_norm = np.linalg.norm(w)

# Compute signed distances for all points
signed_distances = y * (X @ w + b) / w_norm

print(f"\nWeight vector w: {w}")
print(f"Bias b: {b:.4f}")
print(f"||w||: {w_norm:.4f}")

print(f"\nSigned distances (geometric margins):")
print(f"  Min: {signed_distances.min():.4f}")
print(f"  Max: {signed_distances.max():.4f}")
print(f"  Mean: {signed_distances.mean():.4f}")

# Support vectors have margin ≈ 1/||w||
sv_indices = svm.support_
sv_distances = signed_distances[sv_indices]
print(f"\nSupport vector distances:")
print(f"  {sv_distances}")
print(f"  All ≈ {1/w_norm:.4f} = 1/||w||  ✓")

print(f"\nMargin width = 2/||w|| = {2/w_norm:.4f}")

docs.title: Primal Problem
docs.text:
The hard-margin SVM optimization problem:

Minimize:    ½ ||w||²

Subject to:  yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1    for i = 1, ..., n

Intuition: - Objective: Minimize ||w||² ⟺ Maximize margin = 2/||w|| - Constraints: All points correctly classified with margin ≥ 1

Why ||w||² instead of ||w||? - ||w||² is differentiable everywhere - Makes optimization convex quadratic (easier to solve) - Factor ½ makes derivative cleaner

docs.title: Constraint Normalization
docs.text:
Why the constraint yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1 and not yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ γ?

The "1" is a normalization convention:

If (w, b) satisfies  yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ γ
Then (w/γ, b/γ) satisfies  yᵢ((w/γ)ᵀxᵢ + b/γ) ≥ 1

We can always rescale to make the margin equal 1.
This eliminates one degree of freedom and simplifies the problem.

docs.title: Geometric Margin in Terms of w
docs.text:
From yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1:

Geometric margin = 1 / ||w||

Therefore:
  Maximize margin  ⟺  Maximize 1/||w||
                    ⟺  Minimize ||w||
                    ⟺  Minimize ½||w||²

The last form is preferred because it's a quadratic function.

docs.title: Problem Classification
docs.text:
The hard-margin SVM is a Convex Quadratic Program (QP):

Minimize:    f(w) = ½||w||² = ½wᵀw        (convex quadratic objective)

Subject to:  gᵢ(w,b) = 1 - yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≤ 0    (linear constraints)

Key properties: 1. Convex: Objective is convex, constraints are convex 2. Quadratic: Objective is quadratic in w 3. Linear constraints: Each constraint is a linear inequality 4. Unique solution: Convex QP has unique global minimum

docs.title: Lagrangian Formulation
docs.text:
Introduce Lagrange multipliers αᵢ ≥ 0:

L(w, b, α) = ½||w||² - Σᵢ αᵢ[yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) - 1]

           = ½||w||² - Σᵢ αᵢyᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) + Σᵢ αᵢ

docs.title: Dual Problem Derivation
docs.text:
Step 1: Set derivatives to zero:

∂L/∂w = 0:   w - Σᵢ αᵢyᵢxᵢ = 0
              ⟹  w = Σᵢ αᵢyᵢxᵢ

∂L/∂b = 0:   -Σᵢ αᵢyᵢ = 0
              ⟹  Σᵢ αᵢyᵢ = 0

Step 2: Substitute back into Lagrangian:

L_dual(α) = Σᵢ αᵢ - ½ Σᵢ Σⱼ αᵢαⱼyᵢyⱼ(xᵢᵀxⱼ)

Step 3: Dual optimization problem:

Maximize:    W(α) = Σᵢ αᵢ - ½ Σᵢ Σⱼ αᵢαⱼyᵢyⱼ(xᵢᵀxⱼ)

Subject to:  Σᵢ αᵢyᵢ = 0
             αᵢ ≥ 0    for i = 1, ..., n

docs.title: KKT Conditions
docs.text:
The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions are necessary and sufficient for optimality:

1. Stationarity:
   w = Σᵢ αᵢyᵢxᵢ
   Σᵢ αᵢyᵢ = 0

2. Primal feasibility:
   yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1    ∀i

3. Dual feasibility:
   αᵢ ≥ 0    ∀i

4. Complementary slackness:
   αᵢ[yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) - 1] = 0    ∀i

Key insight from complementary slackness:

Either:  αᵢ = 0     →  Point is not a support vector
Or:      yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) = 1  →  Point is exactly on the margin

docs.title: Small Example: 2D Linearly Separable
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

# Simple 2D example
X_simple = np.array([[1, 1], [2, 2], [2, 0],  # Class +1
                     [-1, -1], [-2, -2], [-2, 0]])  # Class -1
y_simple = np.array([1, 1, 1, -1, -1, -1])

print("="*60)
print("HARD-MARGIN SVM: MANUAL SOLUTION")
print("="*60)
print(f"\nData shape: {X_simple.shape}")
print(f"Classes: {np.unique(y_simple)}")

# Dual objective: max Σαᵢ - ½ΣΣ αᵢαⱼyᵢyⱼxᵢᵀxⱼ
# Convert to minimization: min -Σαᵢ + ½ΣΣ αᵢαⱼyᵢyⱼxᵢᵀxⱼ
def dual_objective(alpha, X, y):
    n = len(y)
    K = X @ X.T  # Kernel matrix (linear kernel)

    # Objective: -Σαᵢ + ½ΣΣ αᵢαⱼyᵢyⱼK(xᵢ,xⱼ)
    term1 = -np.sum(alpha)
    term2 = 0.5 * np.sum((alpha * y).reshape(-1, 1) @ 
                         (alpha * y).reshape(1, -1) * K)
    return term1 + term2

# Constraints
from scipy.optimize import LinearConstraint, Bounds

# Equality: Σαᵢyᵢ = 0
eq_constraint = LinearConstraint(y_simple, 0, 0)

# Bounds: αᵢ ≥ 0
bounds = Bounds(0, np.inf)

# Initial guess
alpha0 = np.zeros(len(y_simple))

# Solve
result = minimize(dual_objective, alpha0, args=(X_simple, y_simple),
                  method='SLSQP', constraints=eq_constraint, bounds=bounds)

alpha_sol = result.x

print(f"\nOptimization success: {result.success}")
print(f"Alpha values: {alpha_sol.round(4)}")

# Recover w and b
w_sol = np.sum((alpha_sol * y_simple).reshape(-1, 1) * X_simple, axis=0)
print(f"\nWeight vector w: {w_sol}")

# Compute b from support vectors (where αᵢ > 0)
sv_mask = alpha_sol > 1e-4
b_sol = np.mean(y_simple[sv_mask] - X_simple[sv_mask] @ w_sol)
print(f"Bias b: {b_sol:.4f}")

# Verify constraints
margins = y_simple * (X_simple @ w_sol + b_sol)
print(f"\nMargins yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b):")
print(margins.round(4))
print(f"All ≥ 1: {np.all(margins >= 0.99)}")

print(f"\nSupport vectors (αᵢ > 0):")
print(f"  Indices: {np.where(sv_mask)[0]}")
print(f"  Alpha values: {alpha_sol[sv_mask].round(4)}")

# Compare with sklearn
from sklearn.svm import SVC
svm_check = SVC(kernel='linear', C=1e6)
svm_check.fit(X_simple, y_simple)

print(f"\nsklearn w: {svm_check.coef_[0]}")
print(f"sklearn b: {svm_check.intercept_[0]:.4f}")
print(f"Our w:     {w_sol}")
print(f"Our b:     {b_sol:.4f}")

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Support vectors are the training points that lie exactly on the margin boundaries (where yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) = 1).

Properties of support vectors:
1. αᵢ > 0  (non-zero dual coefficient)
2. Lie on the margin boundary
3. Determine the decision boundary
4. Removing non-support vectors doesn't change the solution

docs.title: Why "Support" Vectors?
docs.text:
The decision function is:

f(x) = sign(wᵀx + b) = sign(Σᵢ αᵢyᵢxᵢᵀx + b)

Since αᵢ = 0 for non-support vectors:

f(x) = sign(Σ_{i∈SV} αᵢyᵢxᵢᵀx + b)

Only support vectors "support" (define) the hyperplane!

docs.title: Visual Analysis
docs.text:
# Analyze support vectors in detail
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

# Panel 1: Annotated support vectors
ax = axes[0]

# Highlight and annotate support vectors
for i, (sv_point, alpha_val) in enumerate(zip(svm.support_vectors_, 
                                               np.abs(svm.dual_coef_[0]))):

               edgecolors='gold', linewidths=3)

                xytext=(sv_point[0]+0.3, sv_point[1]+0.3),
                fontsize=9, color='darkgreen',
                bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor='yellow', alpha=0.7))

ax.set_xlim(-3, 3); ax.set_ylim(-3, 3)

# Panel 2: Distance distribution
ax = axes[1]
all_distances = signed_distances
sv_distances = signed_distances[sv_indices]
nonsv_distances = np.delete(signed_distances, sv_indices)

ax.hist(nonsv_distances, bins=15, alpha=0.6, color='gray', 
        label=f'Non-SV (n={len(nonsv_distances)})')
ax.hist(sv_distances, bins=5, alpha=0.8, color='gold',
        label=f'Support Vectors (n={len(sv_distances)})')
ax.axvline(x=1/w_norm, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=2,

ax.set_ylabel('Count')

ax.legend()
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Statistics

print("SUPPORT VECTOR STATISTICS")

print(f"Total training points: {len(X)}")
print(f"Support vectors: {len(sv_indices)} ({len(sv_indices)/len(X)*100:.1f}%)")
print(f"Non-support vectors: {len(X) - len(sv_indices)}")
print(f"\nSupport vector distances: {sv_distances.round(4)}")
print(f"Expected distance (1/||w||): {1/w_norm:.4f}")

docs.title: When Hard-Margin Fails
docs.text:
Hard-margin SVM requires:
1. Data must be PERFECTLY linearly separable
2. No noise or outliers can exist in the data
3. All constraints yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1 must be satisfiable

If data is not separable → NO SOLUTION EXISTS

docs.title: Demonstration: Non-Separable Data
docs.text:
# Create non-separable data
np.random.seed(42)
X_nonsep = np.vstack([
    np.random.randn(40, 2) + [2, 2],    # Class +1 cluster
    np.random.randn(40, 2) + [-2, -2],  # Class -1 cluster  
    np.random.randn(10, 2)               # Noise in the middle
])
y_nonsep = np.array([1]*40 + [-1]*40 + [1]*5 + [-1]*5)
y_nonsep = np.where(y_nonsep == 0, -1, 1)

print("="*60)
print("HARD-MARGIN SVM ON NON-SEPARABLE DATA")
print("="*60)

# Try hard-margin SVM (large C approximates hard margin)
try:
    svm_hard = SVC(kernel='linear', C=1e6)
    svm_hard.fit(X_nonsep, y_nonsep)
    print(f"Training accuracy: {svm_hard.score(X_nonsep, y_nonsep)*100:.1f}%")

    # Check if any points violate margin
    w_h = svm_hard.coef_[0]
    b_h = svm_hard.intercept_[0]
    margins_h = y_nonsep * (X_nonsep @ w_h + b_h)
    violations = np.sum(margins_h < 0.99)
    print(f"Margin violations: {violations}/{len(X_nonsep)}")

    if violations > 0:
        print("→ Hard-margin SVM failed! Some points inside margin.")
except:
    print("Hard-margin SVM failed to converge!")

print("\nSOLUTION: Use Soft-Margin SVM (Chapter 08)")

docs.title: Three Failure Modes
docs.text:
1. OVERLAPPING CLASSES
   • Classes mixed together in feature space
   • No linear separator exists
   • Solution: Soft margin or non-linear kernel

2. OUTLIERS
   • One or two mislabeled or noisy points
   • Would require very complex boundary to accommodate
   • Solution: Soft margin (allow some violations)

3. NON-LINEAR PATTERNS
   • Data separated by curved boundary
   • Linear separator doesn't exist
   • Solution: Kernel trick (Chapter 09)

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
HARD-MARGIN SVM:

Goal:
  Find the hyperplane that maximally separates linearly separable data

Optimization:
  Minimize:   ½||w||²
  Subject to: yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1    ∀i

Geometric Meaning:
  Margin = 2/||w||
  Maximize margin ⟺ Minimize ||w||

Dual Problem:
  Maximize:   Σαᵢ - ½ΣΣ αᵢαⱼyᵢyⱼxᵢᵀxⱼ
  Subject to: Σαᵢyᵢ = 0,  αᵢ ≥ 0

Decision Function:
  f(x) = sign(wᵀx + b) = sign(Σᵢ αᵢyᵢxᵢᵀx + b)

Support Vectors:
  Points with αᵢ > 0
  Lie exactly on margin boundaries
  Determine the decision boundary

docs.title: Advantages vs Disadvantages
docs.text:
ADVANTAGES:
✓ Unique global optimum (convex optimization)
✓ Principled: maximum margin → good generalization
✓ Sparse solution (only support vectors matter)
✓ Theoretically well-founded

DISADVANTAGES:
✗ Requires perfect linear separability
✗ Sensitive to outliers
✗ No solution exists if data not separable
✗ Only works for linearly separable problems

docs.title: What's Next
docs.text:
Hard-Margin SVM limitations → Soft-Margin SVM (Chapter 08)

Soft-Margin adds:
  • Slack variables ξᵢ to allow violations
  • Parameter C to control margin vs violations trade-off
  • Works on non-separable data

Then: Kernel Trick (Chapter 09)
  • Handle non-linear patterns
  • Apply soft-margin SVM in transformed space
